    Desk · special treatment above 60

    The Spotlight

    Every lead the board grades 60 or better gets a full strategy profile: the setup and the dated catalyst, what the options market is pricing against what the name actually does, a table of eleven structures priced off the real chain and scored twice, and the nine conditions — intraday · swing · long-term against conservative · moderate · aggressive — with a named instrument or an honest "no position" in every cell. Research output; nothing here places an order.

    A spotlight is the long-form version of a lead. The morning book gives you twenty cards with a grade, a thesis and a bracket; a spotlight takes one of those names and writes the document a desk would write about it — where the tape actually is, what is on the calendar and when, what the options market has priced into the print, eleven ways to express the view with the real contracts and their real costs, and then a 3 × 3 table that answers the only question the card cannot: what does this mean for me, at my horizon, at my risk? It exists because a grade of 74 tells you the room liked something and nothing else.

    Research output — model opinion, not financial advice. A spotlight prices structures, scores them and names one. It is a study, not a recommendation, and it is frequently wrong. Every premium in it is a last-traded mark, not a live quote. Nothing in the spotlight — no cell of the nine, no recommended structure, no button on the page — places, stages or routes an order of any kind. Options can expire worthless and defined-risk structures lose their full defined risk regularly.

    What triggers a spotlight#

    One number: 60. Every lead in a completed run whose final grade is 60 or better gets a spotlight — the threshold is the setting spotlight_min_grade, and its default is deliberately the same line as the Fund's admission rule, fund_min_grade. That is not a coincidence and it is not two settings that happen to agree: the owner asked for "special treatment for every stock above sixty", and the system already had a sixty. A lead at 60 is admitted to the Fund and written up as a spotlight on the same morning, off the same grade, so "above sixty" means exactly one thing in this app.

    Sixty is one line, in two places. spotlight_min_grade (default 60) and fund_min_grade (default 60) are separate keys so you can move one without the other — raise the spotlight line to 70 if you only want the strongest names written up — but out of the box they are the same number, and the guide describes the default. Below the line: a card, a bracket and a memo, as before. At or above it: all of that, plus the document on this page.
    When it fires
    After a morning run has persisted — a pipeline hook at the end of the run, not during grading, so a failed spotlight can never damage a briefing. The hook writes up to spotlight_max_per_run profiles (default 8) in one pass, because each one pulls its own option chains; the rest of the ≥60 book is a generate click away. The whole hook is behind spotlight_enabled (default on).
    On demand
    POST /api/spotlight/<lead_id>/generate (authenticated) rebuilds one, at today's prices, for any lead — including one that has since fallen below the line, so you can ask for the study on a name the board graded 58.
    On a re-run
    One row per lead per run, upserted: regenerating replaces that lead's spotlight rather than stacking a second copy. The document always carries its own as-of date and time, and the page prints it in the same large date block the dashboard uses, because a spotlight priced on Friday is a different document by Monday.
    In mock mode
    It generates. The chain, the levels and the earnings history are market data, not model calls, so the structure table is real without an API key; the board's split and the written argument fall back to the deterministic personas like every other session.

    The badge on the card#

    You never have to go looking. A lead with a spotlight carries a small SPOTLIGHT chip next to its grade, titled "graded above 60 — a full strategy profile exists"; clicking the chip opens the profile at #/spotlight/<lead_id>. The same chip appears in four other places, so the fact never gets lost between surfaces:

    • on the lead card in the morning book, beside the final grade and the horizon chip;
    • in the Archive's day view, on the same cards, so a past day says which of its names were written up;
    • in the Fund's holdings table, on a lot whose lead was spotlighted — the two are triggered by the same grade, so most Fund lots have one;
    • in the briefing PDF, as the word SPOTLIGHT after the grade in that lead's block.

    And the dashboard carries a Spotlights strip listing the day's spotlighted names, so the answer to "which names got the full treatment today" is one glance, not twenty cards.

    A profile you asked for, marked as such#

    The generate endpoint will build a profile for any lead, including one the board graded below the line — that is deliberate, because "write me the study on the name you graded 58" is a reasonable thing to want. But a strip that lists an asked-for profile alongside earned ones, under a heading claiming everything in it cleared sixty, is lying about the second kind.

    So a below-the-line profile is marked: its chip is dashed, flagged on request, and its tooltip reads "below the 60.0 line, generated on request". The strip's own caption counts the two kinds separately rather than asserting they are the same thing.

    The distinction that made this necessary. On 2026-08-25 the app's own mock run graded NKE at 59.9, the card rounded it to 60, and the obvious question was why it had no Spotlight. The answer was that it never cleared the line — the display had. Grades now carry one decimal, and a profile generated anyway says it was asked for.

    The nine conditions#

    This is the part the owner asked for by name: "short, medium, long term — intraday, swing, long term — and a table mapping that into conservative, moderate, aggressive, so it's here's what you should do in these nine conditions." It is a 3 × 3 table. Rows are your horizon; columns are your risk.

    The important thing about the grid is what it is made of. Neither axis is invented for this page. Both are house tables that were already load-bearing elsewhere in the app, and the spotlight derives the nine cells from them:

    AxisValuesSourceWhat it already does
    Rows — horizonintraday 0–5 DTE · swing 6–30 · long_term 45–180config.CLASS_DTE (round 25)The mandate's own contract windows: the days-to-expiry band the options scanner may pick from for a lead of that horizon class.
    Columns — riskconservative 1.0 / 1.5 · moderate 1.5 / 2.5 · aggressive 2.0 / 4.0 (stop / target, in ATR)pulse.goals.EXIT_ZONE_ATRThe Pulse's exit brackets and the stop/target on every lead card — the same arithmetic, from the same constant.

    So a cell is not a new opinion about risk. It is the intersection of a window the scanner already respects and a bracket the desk already prints: the aggressive swing cell means "a contract from the 6–30 day window, stopped at 2.0 ATR and targeted at 4.0 ATR". If you change your risk profile on the Pulse, the columns do not move — the bracket multiples are constants — but which cell is yours does.

    What one cell carries#

    Every cell — including the ones that say no — carries the same fields, so the nine are comparable at a glance:

    instrument
    Shares, or a named contract from the chain that was actually pulled for this name in that DTE window (expiry, strike, call/put), through the same options_scanner.pick_contract the morning book uses. No cell ever cites a contract that does not exist in the pull.
    structure
    Outright, debit spread, credit spread, condor, collar, barbell — or "no position", with the reason.
    entry reference
    The price the cell is anchored on: the lead's entry for shares, the contract's last-traded mark for options.
    stop · target
    As prices, from EXIT_ZONE_ATR at that column's multiples, direction-signed on the underlying — the same function the card's levels strip uses, so a spotlight can never print a different stop from the card it came from.
    move required
    The distance to the target as a percentage of the entry, so the aggressive row's 4.0 ATR is legible as "this needs +9.4%" rather than as a multiple.
    size hint
    Small · medium · large, from your size goal. A hint about proportion, not a position size, and never a dollar amount.
    what it needs to win
    One sentence. "Needs the print to land inside 205–225 by Friday" is a cell you can check yourself; "bullish" is not.
    viable · reason
    A flag with prose. When the chain cannot support the cell the spotlight falls back and says so — the commonest case is a name with no 45–180 DTE listings, where the long-term row becomes shares with the same ATR bracket and the cell reads "no 45–180 DTE chain for this name; shares instead".

    Why a cell says "no position"#

    Because the honest answer to "what should I do intraday with a name whose catalyst is on Wednesday night" is nothing, and a table that fills all nine boxes no matter what is a table that has stopped telling you the truth. A cell that should not be traded says no position and gives the reason; it does not manufacture a scalp so the grid looks complete.

    The reasons that actually occur, in rough order of frequency:

    • The catalyst is outside the window. The whole intraday row on a name whose print is three sessions away. This is the common one, and the NVDA study is exactly it — on the Monday, nothing about NVIDIA resolves inside a single session.
    • The bracket is inside the noise. A conservative 1.0 ATR stop on a name whose implied move is 6% is a stop that the event itself will take out; the cell says that rather than pretending the bracket survives the print.
    • The chain will not support it. No listings in the window, or nothing above the scanner's last_price > 0.05 dust floor — the cell falls back to shares and names the gap, or refuses.
    • The structure needs a leg that is not there. A condor whose wing does not exist at a sane strike is not a condor; it is an uncovered short, and the spotlight will not print one.

    Your own cell is highlighted — and the other eight stay#

    The page reads your pulse_risk and pulse_size settings and the run's mandate, rings the cell that matches, and labels it "this is your stated profile". The other eight are still on the page, still fully priced. That is deliberate and it is what the owner asked for: nine conditions, not one recommendation dressed up as nine. Your stated profile is a setting you chose in thirty seconds, and the fastest way to notice that it no longer fits is to see what the room would have written for the other eight.

    The structure study#

    Under the grid sits the part a card can never carry: every plausible way to express the view, priced against each other. The spotlight prices up to eleven candidate structures off the chain that was actually pulled — long call and long put, debit spread, credit spread, straddle, strangle, iron condor, broken-wing condor, calendar, and the barbell (a condor body plus a cheap tail ticket) — plus, always, the board's own lead, so you can see what the room's expression costs beside the alternatives it did not consider.

    For each structure it reports the net debit or credit, maximum win, maximum loss, the break-evens, reward-to-risk — and then the two columns that are the point:

    Under the market's implied distribution
    Probability of profit and expected value, over 40 000 draws from a lognormal (fixed seed, so the same chain always gives the same numbers) whose sigma is the name’s own implied move — the at-the-money straddle divided by spot. This is the market's own opinion about how far the name travels, used to score the structures the market is selling.
    … at each structure's own expiry
    The implied move is a move to a date, so every row is scored at the straddle on its own expiry — printed beside the numbers in the scored at column. A December structure is measured against December's implied move, not next Friday's. This matters more than it sounds: scoring a 116-day spread under a 4-day sigma puts almost every draw inside its wings and turns a losing structure into an apparent near-certainty. The consequence is that PoP and EV are not comparable down the table — a longer-dated row is answering a different question — so compare rows within one expiry and let the per-horizon recommendations do the cross-tenor work. Where an expiry has no at-the-money straddle of its own the front week's is scaled by the square root of time, and the row says so.
    Against the name's own history
    The P&L each structure would actually have produced against that name's last ten earnings reactions, re-priced at each of those ten realised moves. Not a model — arithmetic on ten dates that happened. Only structures that are still alive on the earnings date get this column: a condor expiring on the 28th has no record against a print on the 3rd, and it reads n/a rather than borrowing the ones next to it. "Best by history" is ranked over that subset alone.

    The worked example: NVDA, week of 2026-08-24#

    The reference document this page productises is the NVDA week-of-earnings study in data/boardroom/2026-08-24-nvda/. NVDA closed Friday at 214.72; the 8/28 at-the-money straddle cost 13.25, an implied move of ±6.17%. Its last ten earnings reactions averaged 6.52% absolute — and its last six averaged 4.99%, four of them negative. Volatility, in other words, was priced about right. Here is the study's own table, per one contract, as it came out:

    StructureNetMax winMax lossR:RPOPEV (implied)Last 10Mean (hist)
    A · long straddle 8/28 215+13252997−13222.2731.7%−2734 of 10+81
    B · long strangle 8/28 205P/225C+5452777−5455.1024.2%−2033 of 10−22
    C · iron condor 8/28 195/205/225/235−359359−6410.5669.5%+926 of 10−15
    D · wide iron condor 8/28 190/200/230/240−219219−7810.2880.8%+817 of 10+37
    E · call debit spread 8/28 220/235+3301170−3303.5525.0%−663 of 10+66
    F · put credit spread 8/28 200/190−103103−8970.1188.6%+359 of 10+68
    G · broken-wing condor 8/28 195/205/230/245−321321−11790.2775.1%+1036 of 10−21
    H · call calendar 8/28 215C / 9/04 215C+120362*−1203.0260.0%+704 of 10−3
    I · iron condor 9/04 195/205/225/235−419419−5810.7271.7%+1527 of 10+45
    J · barbell: 9/04 condor + long 8/28 235C−3091562−6912.2670.1%+846 of 10+85
    K · the board's own lead: long 8/28 220C+4403313−4407.5322.5%−1343 of 10+105

    Dollars per contract; a negative Net is a credit collected rather than a debit paid. POP and EV are under the implied distribution; the last two columns are against NVDA's own last ten prints. Every premium in the table is a last-traded mark from a weekend pull, not a live quote.

    * The calendar's maximum is an estimate, not a payoff: the back-week leg is valued at the front-week expiry with Black-Scholes at an assumed post-event volatility of 40% (NVDA's own 20-day realised was 38.3%), and the study reports the 30% and 50% cases beside it. Black-Scholes is used for that one job — valuing a longer-dated leg at a nearer expiry — and every number that depends on it is labelled an estimate wherever it appears.

    How to read it: two columns that disagree#

    The table is built so that the EV (implied) column and the Mean (hist) column can argue, because they usually do. They are two different questions:

    • EV (implied) asks: if the market's own priced distribution is the truth, is this structure worth its cost? A positive number means you are being paid relative to what the crowd charged.
    • Mean (hist) asks: if this name behaves the way it has behaved on its last ten prints, what would this structure have made? A positive number means the name's actual habits favour it.

    Look down the NVDA table and the disagreement is stark. The long straddle (A) is +81 on history but −273 implied — NVDA's big old moves would have paid for it, the market's current pricing would not. The board's own 220 call (K) is the same trade in sharper form: +105 on history, −134 implied, the best historical mean on the menu and a losing bet against the crowd's price. The condors invert it: G is +103 implied but −21 on history, because the two 2024 prints that ran double digits do not care about probability of profit.

    A structure positive in both columns is rare, and that is the column pair's whole job. On this menu, four of the eleven managed it — D, F, I and J — and of those, only the barbell (J) did it while keeping a reward-to-risk above 1. F wins nine times in ten and risks 897 to make 103; D and I are the same shape with better numbers. Being right about direction is cheap; being paid for being right is not. When you read a spotlight, read those two columns together and treat any structure that only clears one of them as a bet on which distribution you believe — not as an edge.

    One structure per horizon, and where it dies#

    The document then does what the NVDA study did: it names one structure per horizon row, says why in a paragraph, and — the part that matters — says where it stops working. For NVDA the recommendation was the barbell, J: sell the 9/04 condor body (short the 205 put and the 225 call, long the 195 and 235 wings), and spend 1.10 of the credit on a single 8/28 235 call.

    The argument was structural, not directional. The 9/04 body sells the fat middle of the distribution where the crowd reliably overpays, and it expires the week after the Friday keynote instead of into it. The 235 call buys back the one outcome that has ever genuinely destroyed a premium seller in this name — February 2024's +16.4% — and it does so cheaply enough to flip that quarter from the worst case to the best: on a repeat of that print the barbell makes +802 where the naked 9/04 condor loses −581. Break-evens 202.03, 228.28 and 242.03 against a 214.72 spot: −5.9%, +6.3% and +12.7%.

    And then, in the document's own words, where it dies: in the medium move. The barbell loses on a 6-to-10% travel in either direction — −664 on a repeat of May 2024's +9.32%, −540 on February 2025's −8.48% — and that zone is exactly where the implied move sits. Maximum loss is 691 per contract, defined at entry, below 195. A spotlight that names a structure without printing that paragraph is not finished.

    What is in the document#

    Both renderings — the JSON the app reads and the PDF you can send — carry the same sections in the same order:

    1. The setup — tape, levels, technicals, gap zone, 52-week context.
    2. The catalyst — dated and sourced, or the honest "none on any calendar". The house primary-source rule applies: a date comes from the issuer's or the agency's own calendar or it does not appear.
    3. What the options market is pricing versus what the name actually does — the implied move against the last ten realised reactions.
    4. The nine conditions — the grid above.
    5. The structure study — the table above.
    6. The recommendation per horizon — one per row, with the reason and where it dies.
    7. The read-across — the round-24 coupling: betas, correlated peers, the implied-move table and the watch-also list, because five leads reading one earnings call is one bet in five slots.
    8. The board's split on the lead — who was high, who was low, and the Skeptic's line, so the disagreement travels with the study.
    9. What could be wrong, and the standing disclaimer.

    The JSON is what the app renders and the API serves; the PDF is the house-style copy you can send, named Bablytics-Spotlight-<TICKER>-<date>.pdf. Every premium column in both carries the same one-line mark note, and every Black-Scholes number the same one-line estimate note — one string each, from one place, so no surface can quietly drop the caveat.

    Where it lives in the app#

    #/spotlight/<lead_id>
    The full profile: the as-of date block, the nine-condition grid as a real table with your cell ringed, the structure table, the recommended structure's payoff as an inline SVG, the read-across, the board split and the caveats.
    The Spotlights strip
    On the dashboard, listing the day's spotlighted names with their grades.
    GET /api/spotlight/<lead_id>
    The payload for one lead.
    GET /api/spotlights?run_id=
    The list for a run.
    POST /api/spotlight/<lead_id>/generate
    Regenerate at today's prices (authenticated).
    GET /api/spotlight/<lead_id>/pdf
    The document.
    spotlights table
    One row per lead per run — run, lead, ticker, as-of, grade, payload and PDF path — upserted on regeneration.
    The knobs
    Four settings rows, read at call time so a change takes effect without a restart: spotlight_enabled (default on), spotlight_min_grade (default 60 — the same number as fund_min_grade), spotlight_max_per_run (default 8) and spotlight_post_iv (default 0.40 — the last-resort post-event volatility for the one Black-Scholes estimate, used only when the name's own back-expiry implied volatility cannot be read at all).
    The PDF
    Bablytics-Spotlight-<TICKER>-<as-of>.pdf under data/reports, collected into runs/ with every other generated document.

    The honest limits#

    A document this specific earns a proportionally specific list of what it cannot do. None of these is a bug; all of them are properties of the data, and the spotlight prints them on its own last page rather than leaving them to this one.

    Every premium is a last-traded mark, not a live quote.
    The chain gives last_price: the price at which that contract most recently traded, which may have been hours or days ago and is not a price anyone is currently offering. The real bid/ask spread is wider than these marks, sometimes much wider, and on a weekend pull the whole table is stale by construction. Nothing in a spotlight is executable at the numbers it prints, and every dollar figure in it should be read as "roughly, at Friday's marks".
    Open interest is often unavailable.
    The OI-conversion audit the desk normally runs on an option lead — the check that catches a crowded or an illiquid structure — needs open interest, and the source returns zero across an entire chain often enough that it must be assumed missing. On the NVDA study it came back zero for every strike, so that check simply could not be run. When it is missing the spotlight says so; it does not silently score liquidity from volume alone.
    Ten prints are a story, not a distribution.
    The historical column is ten dates. Ten is not a sample you can compute a confidence interval from, the two largest moves in the NVDA set are both more than two years old, and a company that has changed size and business mix over those ten quarters is not the same company at each of them. Read that column as "this is what this name has tended to do", never as a probability.
    The implied distribution is an assumption, not a fact.
    The POP and EV columns assume the market's own priced distribution is the true one — lognormal, sigma from the ATM straddle. If that were reliably true no options structure would carry an edge at all, this one included.
    Multi-expiry structures are evaluated at one price.
    The barbell spans two expiries; the payoff table evaluates every leg at a single terminal price, which is a simplification. The nearer leg resolves first, and whatever sits between the two dates — a Fed keynote, in the NVDA case — is not in the arithmetic.
    Black-Scholes appears exactly once, and is labelled.
    Only to value a back-week leg at a front-week expiry, at an assumed post-event volatility. Every number that depends on it says estimate.
    That post-event volatility is the name's own — and it is still the whole trade.
    The calendar's entire case is one number: what the back leg is worth once the event has passed. The study reads that number off this name's own back-expiry at-the-money contracts (the feed's implied volatility, or solved out of the marks when the feed gives none), never a constant borrowed from whichever name the method was written on — a 40% assumption applied to a 28%-vol name is not an estimate, it is fiction, and it can flip the structure's expected value from best-in-document to negative. A house default exists only as a last resort and the row says when it was used. Even so, the sensitivity band beside it — now walked around the volatility actually used rather than around a fixed 30/40/50 — is the honest width of that row, and "where it dies" names it.
    A spotlight is not a second opinion on the grade.
    It is triggered by the grade and does not revisit it. A well-argued spotlight on a lead the board got wrong is a well-argued document about a bad idea.
    Not financial advice. Everything on a spotlight page — the nine cells, the structure table, the recommendation, the payoff diagram — is model output from a research and entertainment tool, produced without any knowledge of your account, your obligations or your tax position. It is not personalized, it is not reviewed by any licensed professional, and it is frequently wrong. Bablytics executes no trades and places no orders on your behalf, and the spotlight package contains no order path of any kind. See Not financial advice.
